title: CLO Tips Workshop - Methods for Handling Hair Occlusion and Seam Stitching
description: A daily tip: CLO technical experts teach you how to handle hair occlusion and seam stitching in four minutes!
transcript:
This time, the technique class will discuss how to handle hair blocking.  
When combing, if the style is similar to a belt that covers the hair band, hair may pass through the belt.  
At the seam area, there also needs to be the effect of hair being pressed by the sewing line.  
In this session, I will talk about the processing techniques for this.  

First, we select the fixing needle tool.  
In the 3D window, make an empty selection; this step is to find the part of the belt covering the clothing.  
Then, when we add the fixing needle, you can see the marks added by the fixing needle on the 2D board.  
The gap in the middle is the part of the belt covering.  
We can choose our basic line tool and draw the base line on it.  
Draw the range of our blocking area.  
This makes it convenient for us to fill in the blanks later.  

While drawing, press the Ctrl key and left-click to create a curve line.  
After adding, we can switch to print mode.  
Here, we find the fabric of the jacket.  
Then we can output the fabric of our jacket here.  
Here is the base line that only needs to be displayed.  
Because the hair has no texture, you can directly select the fabric texture to display the entire version in a solid color.  
Then check the information; this side does not need to be selected.  
Click Save.  

Next, we open our image in Photoshop.  
We can see that the gap in the middle is the part where the belt covers.  
We select this part.  
Then fill it in.  
We can add a layer.  
Fill it with black.  
This will create a dense default image.  
There will be no hair in the black area.  
Hair will appear in the white area.  
All layers will be displayed in one layer.  
Then there will be a beefile (likely “bevel” or “base file”) in the top layer.  
We press the Ctrl key to start a new layer.  
Find one layer here.  
Most layers are black.  
If we select this layer,  
we can see the color is white here.  
We can use this layer with white.  
And we can select a layer where all are black.  

We can select this layer.  
The width of the side can be adjusted accordingly based on the effect.  
In this way, an area can be created on the edge of the board.  
There will be no hair inside.  
Then there will be a hair pressure mark effect.  
At the same time, we can wipe off the side of the collar,  
which is the place without the seal.  

Then, in the same way, we perform this process on other parts.  
After the process is complete, the default image looks like this.  

Finally, let's return to this costume.  
We select the large fabric.  
Then open it in the default image.  
Place the default image we just made into the density column.  
The hair density in the black area will be zero,  
so there will be no hair.  
In the white area, the hair density will maintain its original density.  

In this way, the hair can be processed with the effect of being blocked by the belt.  
Then go to the side seam of the garment.  
You can see that the hair pressure mark effect has also appeared here.  

Today’s class ends here.  
Thank you all.

chunks.title: CLO Tips Workshop - Methods for Handling Hair Occlusion and Seam Stitching
chunks.content: ## Handling Hair Occlusion in CLO: Techniques for Blocking and Seam Stitching Effects This section explains methods in CLO for managing hair occlusion caused by garment elements like belts and seams, focusing on creating realistic hair blocking and pressure effects using tools such as the Fixing Needle, base lines, fabric textures, and default images. ### Identifying and Marking Hair Blocking Areas with the Fixing Needle Tool To handle hair occlusion where a belt covers part of the hair band, start by selecting the Fixing Needle tool in CLO. In the 3D window, make an empty selection to locate the belt area that overlaps the garment and blocks the hair. Once the Fixing Needle is added, its marks appear on the 2D pattern board, revealing the gap where the belt covers the hair. Use the Basic Line tool to draw a baseline along this gap, defining the precise range of the hair blocking area. While drawing, holding the Ctrl key and left-clicking allows you to create curved lines for accurate shaping. This baseline simplifies filling in occlusion areas later in the workflow. ### Setting Fabric Textures and Output for Hair Blocking Visualization Switch to Print Mode to configure fabric outputs for the jacket. Since hair lacks texture, select the jacket’s fabric texture and display it as a solid color version to clearly distinguish between covered and uncovered areas. Unselect any unnecessary parts of the fabric and save the output. This setup prepares the garment fabric for applying hair occlusion masks. ### Creating Hair Blocking Masks in Photoshop Using Default Images Export the fabric image to Photoshop to define hair occlusion zones precisely. The gap where the belt covers the hair appears as a white area, with the rest black. 1. Select the belt coverage area (the white gap). 2. Add a new layer and fill it with black, representing zero hair density—no hair will appear here. 3. Combine all layers into one, ensuring the top layer is the base mask layer. 4. Use Ctrl to add new layers and isolate layers with white regions indicating visible hair. 5. Adjust the width of the edges around the blocking area to create a hair pressure mark effect along the garment edges. 6. Clean up areas like the collar edge where there is no seam seal to refine the mask. Repeat this process on other garment parts where hair is occluded or pressed by seams. ### Applying Default Images to Control Hair Density in CLO Return to CLO and select the large garment fabric. Open the edited default image (mask) and assign it to the Density channel. - Black areas in the default image correspond to zero hair density, effectively removing hair from those regions. - White areas maintain the original hair density, allowing hair to show normally. This method accurately simulates hair being blocked by belts and pressed by seams, producing realistic occlusion and pressure mark effects on hair in CLO garments.
